opinions.rationale: Under an inverted prior, the open components of CNF-01 were treated as likely already closed by method, reporting guidance, or software; searches do not support that closure. The phenomenon itself is long recognized: observational assignment-to-initiate contrasts are confounded at baseline, and later initiation in the non-initiator arm dilutes the observational intention-to-treat (ITT) analogue as follow-up lengthens. Hernán and Hernández-Díaz (Clin Trials 2012; doi:10.1177/1740774511420743) document ITT dilution under nonadherence and argue for careful per-protocol (PP) work in comparative effectiveness. Hernán and Robins (Am J Epidemiol 2016; doi:10.1093/aje/kwv254), already cited, define observational ITT versus PP analogues and what each requires; they do not supply a reporting convention that forces cumulative initiation trajectories in both arms beside the effect estimate, nor a rule for a still-meaningful horizon. Cain et al. (Int J Epidemiol 2016; doi:10.1093/ije/dyv295), also already cited, is the main design response: name later initiation via dynamic strategies rather than an open-ended never-initiate arm. That changes the estimand; it does not identify or “debias” the attenuated ITT contrast under realistic crossover. Recent restatements keep the issue open rather than solved. Terman (Neurology 2025; doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000214269) states that the ITT effect is typically attenuated to the degree patients switch after assignment, with a statin initiator versus noninitiator example where PP was stronger than ITT. Molero-Calafell et al. (J Clin Epidemiol 2024) restate that ITT can dilute effects when adherence differs. TARGET (Cashin et al., JAMA 2025; doi:10.1001/jama.2025.13350) is the strongest recent reporting push: it requires naming the causal contrast (assignment versus adherence), mapping strategies to data, and reporting sensitivity to design and analysis choices. From published summaries of the 21-item checklist, it does not mandate cumulative incidence of treatment initiation in both arms over follow-up as a standard diagnostic of strategy convergence, and it does not establish a horizon convention for when an initiate-now versus not-now contrast remains interpretable. STaRT-RWE, HARPER, NICE RWE framework, FDA RWE/data-source materials, ENCePP, and ICH E9(R1) improve estimand language and protocol structure generally; none close the specific CNF-01 gap that a long-horizon null observational ITT cannot be read against the convergence that produced it. Package checks (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt, riskRegression, adjustedCurves, zEpid, causallib) show outcome cumulative-incidence tools and ITT/PP estimation, not a merged standard for dual-arm treatment-trajectory diagnostics or horizon-linked attenuation simulation. No 2024–2026 paper was found that (i) evaluates a field convention for publishing initiation trajectories beside the ITT estimate, (ii) defines a horizon rule for when the strategies remain distinct enough, or (iii) ships a validated simulation tool mapping observed convergence rates to expected attenuation at each horizon. Proposal and restatement are not resolution. Convergence remains a feature of the ITT strategy contrast under later initiation; PP or dynamic redesigns answer a different question. Status therefore remains open as stated. Queries run: observational ITT attenuation/dilution with later initiation and comparator crossover; target trial emulation treatment trajectories and cumulative initiation in both arms; TARGET/Cashin/Hansford reporting items on adherence and trajectories; Cain/Hernán prior art on dynamic strategies and ITT analogues; arXiv/medRxiv 2024–2026 TTE ITT crossover; CRAN/GitHub activity for TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp and related packages; FDA/EMA/NICE/ENCePP/STaRT-RWE/HARPER 2024–2026 guidance on adherence and ITT in observational emulations.
